title: Leaders Who Pretend to Agree
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece targets a specific form of disloyalty: leaders who appear to support a team decision in the room and then undermine it with their own teams. The author describes the pattern, from telling teams a decision is faulty to instructing them to ignore it, and argues that it sabotages organizational alignment and execution. The central claim is that standing behind a decision one argued against is a defining test of true leadership, and that treating decisions as negotiable is a failure of that test. The piece also notes the cultural cost, a 'we versus they' mentality below. It urges senior leaders to watch how decisions are cascaded and to confront subversion immediately, concluding that such leaders cannot be trusted to lead.
points: Saying 'yes' in the decision meeting and resisting afterward is framed not as creative interpretation but as subversion that fragments organizational effort.
Committing to decisions one opposed is presented as perhaps the most important test of a team leader.
After-the-fact resistance breeds a 'we versus they' mentality in the teams below, eroding culture as well as execution.
Senior leaders should monitor how decisions are explained downstream and confront any leader who trashes a group decision right away.
quotes: One or more of the leaders goes back to their respective teams and informs them of the faulty decision. They make it clear they are not in favor of the decree and then begin to explore how to work around it.

When individual or team agendas take precedence over organization commitments, performance suffers. Leaders who pay lip service to decisions or strategic directions and then do their own thing sabotage the ability of the organization to align and then to execute.
Resisting decisions after they have been made is commonplace in many organizations. Standing squarely for any decision, even those they argued against or disagree with, is a sign of true leadership.

Yet, many leaders don’t view their after-the-decision resistance as anything more than creatively interpreting strategic intent. They convince themselves that team decisions are negotiable and only imply a suggested course of action.

Any time a leader learns that a team member has trashed or subverted the group decision, they must confront this reality immediately. Allowing leaders to do it their way is tantamount to agreeing to fragment the efforts of the larger team.

Leaders who only pretend to agree to team decisions are not to be trusted to lead. Their desire to impose their personal views on a finalized decision suggests they think they know better than the wisdom of the team.
